FULL STORY // ARCHIVE TEXTThe Rise of the Sky Lords

The sky bled red as shadows crawled across the earth, drowning the villages in twilight. Far above, the heavens churned with winged demons, their leathery wings beating against the wind, their screeches splitting the air. These creatures, forged in the abyss, sought dominion over the lands below, hungering for conquest and chaos. Below them, however, stood the only force capable of holding the demonic tide at bay: the warriors.

But these warriors were no longer human, at least not in the way the villagers once knew. Their forms had been twisted, reimagined by powers far greater than mortal comprehension. Once flesh and blood, they had died long ago, only to be summoned back from the grave by the angels. They had been warriors once—now they were something else entirely. Possessed, unholy, vessels of raw, unimaginable power. And though they fought the demons, the villagers feared them almost as much as the monsters they kept at bay.

The warriors moved with a sense of purpose that was unnatural, their eyes glowing with a cold, distant light. They wore the skin and wings of the demons they slaughtered, their bodies grotesque, adorned with trophies of their endless war. There was no mercy in them, no soul behind their gaze. They were bound to the angels, but their own minds, twisted by death and resurrection, surged with a dark and brutal imagination. They fought not out of duty, but for a reason no mortal could fathom.

Far above, an orb of shimmering light floated in the sky, and within it, the angels observed, detached and silent. They watched their creations with a cold curiosity, their celestial forms almost indifferent to the carnage below. The angels did not interfere—they had no need. The warriors were their tools, their instruments of war, and they had been shaped to perfection. What had once been human was now divine, filled with a brutal grace and relentless hunger for violence.

Cynar, the leader of the warriors, stood at the forefront. His face, twisted into a grim mask, was barely recognizable as human. He wore the wings of a demon across his back, a grotesque cloak that dragged across the ground. In his eyes, the light of the angels burned, but something darker stirred beneath it—his own will, his own twisted power, born from countless resurrections. He raised his sword, its edge glinting with the blood of the beasts they had slain.

“They come again,” Cynar muttered, his voice an eerie whisper, barely human. Around him, the warriors shifted, their movements precise, mechanical, like machines awaiting orders. There was no need for speech among them. They were bound by something far deeper, their minds linked through the angels’ will.

In the distance, the demons descended, a black tide of wings and talons. Their leader, a colossal beast wreathed in fire, let out a scream that rattled the earth. But the warriors did not flinch. They had faced these creatures countless times, and each battle only strengthened their resolve. The demons were nothing more than cattle to be slaughtered.

Without a word, Cynar leaped onto his dragon—a beast as twisted as its rider. Once wild, the dragon’s mind had been broken and bent to Cynar’s will, its savage instincts suppressed by ancient magic. With a screech, it took to the sky, and the other warriors followed suit, their dragons roaring into the heavens.

The clash of battle was savage. Fire and steel met claw and fang, the air thick with the stench of burning flesh. Cynar cut through the demons with brutal efficiency, his sword slicing through their wings, tearing them from the sky. Each strike was deliberate, precise—every fallen demon became part of his grotesque collection, their wings lashed to his armor, their carcasses discarded like broken toys.

Around him, the other warriors fought with the same cold precision, their dragons twisting through the air, their claws rending demon flesh. For every demon that fell, another rose, but the warriors did not tire, did not falter. They could not die—they had already passed through death once, and the angels had given them something far worse than mortality: immortality bound to endless slaughter.

Cynar’s dragon soared through the sky, dodging a volley of fiery breath from a demon. With a roar, he raised his hand, channeling the dark magic gifted to him by the angels. His eyes locked onto a demon leader, its wings outstretched as it prepared to attack. Cynar whispered a single command in the ancient tongue of the angels, and the demon froze, its body trembling as its mind was wiped clean. It dropped from the sky, landing at Cynar’s feet, now a mindless slave.

"You're mine," Cynar snarled, mounting the demon like a broken beast. He turned it against its own kind, sending it to tear through the ranks of its former brethren. This was his power—the power of possession, the ability to twist even his enemies into tools for his war. And he relished it.

The battle raged on as the sky darkened further, the village below forgotten in the chaos. No one dared come near the warriors, not even the boldest of villagers. They were more feared than revered, more nightmare than hero. To the villagers, they were ghosts—beings that lingered on the edge of life and death, serving the angels' will, but beyond anyone’s control.

Above them, the angels continued to observe. They whispered to each other, their voices carried on the wind, their words beyond mortal comprehension.

“They are perfect,” one of the angels murmured, its eyes fixed on Cynar and his brutal display.

“Their will grows,” another replied. “But they remain ours. For now.”

“They will fight as long as the demons rise,” the first angel said. “And when the demons are gone, we will find them another war.”

Below, Cynar let out a guttural roar as he tore the wings from another demon, casting its broken body to the ground. He raised his blade high, his bloodstained face lifted toward the orb in the sky.

“We are your sword!” he bellowed, his voice carrying across the battlefield.

But even as he spoke the words, a dark satisfaction curled within him. He was no mere tool, no simple puppet. He was something else—something born of both angelic design and his own ruthless ambition.

The battle continued until the last demon was slain, its wings torn and scattered across the field. The warriors stood among the carnage, their armor slick with blood, their eyes still burning with the same cold light. But there was no victory in their gaze, only a quiet hunger. They would fight again—because that was all they knew.

The villagers would whisper of them in hushed tones, afraid to speak their names too loudly, for fear they might be called upon. The angels watched from their distant perch, ever calculating, ever guiding. But Cynar and his warriors, they knew the truth.

They were more than warriors. They were the embodiment of a darker power, one that even the angels could not fully control.

And as long as the sky burned, they would remain.
